adds.title: LGBTQ rights in Turkey - Wikipedia
adds.summary: Wikipedia's Turkey country overview documents the national framework every visitor to Gümüşhane stands under: homosexuality has not been a criminal offence since the Ottoman Empire's 1858 penal code, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988 (gender-reassignment surgery has been legal since 1988, subject to court-approved procedures). It reports no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and no legal recognition of same-sex relationships: marriage is defined by law as a union between a man and a woman, making same-sex marriage legally impossible though not criminalised, with the gender on a trans person's civil-registry record determining their marriage eligibility. It documents that authorities have banned Pride events in Istanbul and other cities in most years since 2015, with police use of tear gas and water cannons, and Amnesty International reporting restrictions and excessive force against Pride protesters (2015 and 2024 reports). This confirms the record's claim that the national frame, not any provincial legal divergence, governs a trans visitor's exposure in Gümüşhane.

adds.title: LGBTQ rights in Turkey - Wikipedia
adds.summary: Wikipedia's Turkey country overview documents the national framework a visitor to Hakkâri stands under, with no separate provincial layer: homosexuality has not been a criminal offence since the Ottoman Empire's 1858 penal code, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988 (gender-reassignment surgery legal since 1988, court-approved). It reports no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and no legal recognition of same-sex relationships: marriage is defined by law as a union between a man and a woman, making same-sex marriage legally impossible though not criminalised, marriage eligibility turning on the gender in a person's civil-registry record rather than trans status. It documents bans on Pride events in Istanbul and other cities in most years since 2015, with police tear gas and water cannons and Amnesty International reporting restrictions and excessive force (2015 and 2024 reports). This supports the record's claim that Hakkâri's divergence from the national baseline is a matter of security practice and social climate, not trans-specific provincial law.
